catalog_quote: Isenye has only two tonal patterns, namely a H tone on the first syllable of the stem or a H tone linked to all syllables of the stem (7). The domain of the lexical tone is the nominal stem; noun class prefixes are toneless. Isenye nouns satisfies the stress-related criterion of obligatoriness (every word has at least one syllable with the highest prominence) but not culminativity, since multiply linked H (‘all H’) tones are allowed. Both H tones are aligned with the left edge of the stem, which can be viewed as a metrical restriction (Downing 2004). ... With this rather restricted tonal system it is possible that Isenye is changing from a tonal system towards a system with regular stress, possibly under the influence of the national language Swahili, which has regular penultimate stress. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and domain quote are verbatim in the held Aunio 2015 text at the stated proof pages. (2) Deciding source is a 2015 peer-reviewed tone article by the principal fieldworker on these varieties; Glottolog's live bibliography (3 items) and Laine 2023's literature review show nothing better exists for Isenye prosody, and no instrumental or monograph-length phonology exists. (3) Laine 2023 (open, fetched sources to independently restates the system as privative H/zero tone with syllable TBU, two nominal patterns in Ishenyi, toneless verb roots with melodic H, and attributes a stress analysis only to Nata, confirming TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT for isse1238. Remaining unheld items (Aunio 2017, Aunio et al. 2019) are paywalled overviews by the same author and would at most refine the verbal-tone note. Identity: Isenye/I

sources.quote: 'Ws has a privative tone system (i.e. it can be analysed as having a distinction between h and (zero) tone ...), and the tone bearing unit is the syllable ... Ishenyi only has two nominal tonal patterns: a high tone on the first syllable of the stem, or on all stem syllables (Aunio 2015:5). Nata, on the other hand, can (and must) only have one high toned syllable per word, and is thus analysed as a stress system by Anghelescu (2012).' Also: 'Unlike nouns, verbs do not have lexical tonal contrasts. Verb roots are toneless, and infinitive forms have a melodic high tone on the first syllable of .
